title: Visual Search Laboratory
summary: Learners search original geometric displays for a bar that is tilted and solid. In the feature condition it is the only tilted item; in the conjunction condition half the distractors are tilted and half are solid, so neither property alone identifies it. Set size, target presence, search slopes and target-absent trials are all reported, alongside an untimed panel for looking at displays and a seeded worked example that reaches every conclusion without performing the task.
learningObjectives: Define feature and conjunction search in terms of how the target is specified relative to the distractors.
Read a search function and state its slope in milliseconds per item.
Explain why target-absent trials usually give a steeper slope than target-present trials.
Distinguish a description of a search function from a mechanistic claim about parallel or serial processing.
Recognise how few trials per cell a classroom block provides, and what that does to a slope estimate.
interactionTypes: untimed display inspection with target reveal
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; displays are generated and trials timed in the browser tab only, nothing survives a reset, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: The two properties that define the stimuli are orientation (upright or tilted) and fill (solid or hollow). Neither is a colour, so the paradigm works unchanged in greyscale, with any colour vision deficiency, and in forced-colours mode - no substitute encoding is needed. No trial is timed out: the display persists until answered, nothing animates and nothing flashes. An untimed inspection panel comes before the experiment, where a display can be examined at leisure and the target revealed on request, described in words as well as ringed. Four untimed practice trials with feedback precede the scored block. Responses accept the J and F keys or two buttons at least 3.5rem tall. A complete non-timed route exists and is signposted before the task: the seeded worked example fills the results panel for both conditions on its own. The scored display is aria-hidden because a spoken description would give the answer away and arrive too late to be a search. Charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables; the two series differ by line style, marker shape and an inline word. Every control has an accessible name; headings do not skip; focus moves to the results heading when a block ends. Usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Feature and conjunction search: set size, search slopes, and what a slope does not prove
simulationNotes: Displays are generated fresh each time from an 8 by 5 grid with per-item jitter, so nothing sits in a predictable place. Set sizes are 8, 16 and 32, half the trials have no target, and a learner's block is 3 trials per cell (18 trials per condition), which is far too few for a stable slope and is described as such throughout. Responses under 200 ms and over 10000 ms are counted, reported and excluded; only correct trials contribute to reaction-time means; slopes are fitted by ordinary least squares to trial-level data. The worked example uses RT = intercept + slope * setSize + Normal(0, sd) + Exponential(tail), with feature intercept 430 and slopes 1.5 (present) and 2.5 (absent), sd 70 and tail 60; conjunction intercept 470 and slopes 24 and 46, sd 90 and tail 70; accuracies .98/.98 and .94/.96; 14 trials per cell per condition with fixed seed 20260825. It produces feature slopes of 2.7 (present) and 3.9 (absent) ms per item and conjunction slopes of 22.4 and 45.2 ms per item. The roughly two-to-one ratio between absent and present slopes is built into the generator rather than discovered, and the page says so: the example illustrates the pattern, it does not evidence it. No parameter here is a norm, a published estimate or anybody's data. Browser timing carries tens of milliseconds of noise, and display size and item spacing are uncontrolled, both of which change search efficiency.
